newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FEATURE - Banco Pactual bets on Brazil's future.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Banco Pactual bets on Brazil's future.

text.p: Luiz Cesar Fernandes, the 52-year-old chief of Brazil's feisty investment bank Pactual, has worked in financial markets since he was 12 and in that time he has seen economic plans come and go.
But Fernandes says the prosperity generated by Brazil's most recent economic programme, the Real Plan, is here to stay.

While some Brazil watchers are beginning to question how long the latest "economic miracle" will last, Fernandes is confident there is no going back to the hyperinflation and economic chaos that once characterized Brazil.
"The risk of returning to the past is zero. Whoever bets against that is going to lose," Fernandes told Reuters.
He ought to know.

Despite having no formal training in business or finance, he has built up the strongest competitor to Brazil's premier investment bank, Garantia -- recognized at home and abroad for its aggressiveness on the trading floor and at the negotiating table.
FROM OFFICE BOY TO PRESIDENT
Fernandes, who started his long career as an office boy running papers from one desk to another at a huge federal bank in Sao Paulo, was one of three partners to found Garantia in 1971.
But he left the bank in the early 1980s to start his own business and realize an ambition nursed since his teens.
"I wanted to be president," Fernandes explains.

Today the Rio de Janeiro-based bank leads the business in restructuring troubled companies and financial institutions. Among Brazilian investment banks, it is second only to Garantia in Brady bond trading, at $16 billion a year, and is a leading market maker in stocks and domestic debt.
Pactual, with a staff of 365, is also strong in asset management, with some $3.8 billion under administration. Its businesses this year should turn a $250 million net profit, according to Fernandes.
FORTUNES REAPED UNDER LOW INFLATION

Brazil's inflation-slashing Real Plan, which turned three years old in July, was largely to thank for the enormous profits made by Pactual and other Brazilian investment banks over the past few years.
Slashing annual inflation from 3,000 percent to single digits has taken its toll on Brazil's retail banking sector, which had grown fat on easy arbitrage opportunities under hyperinflation.
Big name retail banks like Nacional, Economico and Bamerindus were forced to merge with healthier institutions better prepared to deal with the new low-inflation reality.

But that same reality has been a boon for investment banks, which have reaped fortunes underwriting a record number of equity and debt issues and restructuring companies unaccustomed to the new way of doing business.

The flurry of activity has attracted top names in U.S. investment banking, including recent arrivals Prudential Securities and Morgan Stanley Dean Witter, which have opened offices in Sao Paulo in the past three months.
The onslaught of U.S. banks has pressured an already competitive market, but Fernandes says he is not worried about Pactual's future.
FAMILY BUSINESSES NEED HELP SELLING OUT

The bank has made a name for itself helping third- and fourth-generation family businesses -- which lack the expertise to compete with multinationals and leaner local firms -- sell out to larger groups.
Such sales, Fernandes says, will keep Pactual busy well into the next century.

"Unlike Mexico or other Latin American countries where there are just a handful of families controlling all businesses, Brazil has thousands of family-run businesses with revenues ranging from a few thousand to billions of dollars," he said.
Brazilian banks have an edge over foreigners in arranging the sale of these businesses because the families prefer working with other Brazilians, Fernandes said.
He noted that local banks are also much more knowledgeable about the inner workings of Brazilian corporate law, which many foreign banks would just as soon leave alone.
Pactual recently restructured ailing retailer Mesbla and lined up its sale to entrepreneur Ricardo Mansur, who owns the competing retail chain Mappin, a unit of Casa Anglo.
FOREIGN INTEREST IN BRAZILIAN COMPANIES GROWS
Pactual manages about eight to 10 similar deals a year. And while Brazilian investors have in the past made up the bulk of buyers, foreign participation is growing sharply.

A recent study by KPMG Peat Marwick said 172 mergers and acquisitions had taken place in Brazil in the first half of 1997, with half of those involving foreign firms. In 1996, foreign firms participated in 165 mergers or acquisitions, 27 percent higher than the year before, according to KPMG.

"Despite the difficulties of these family businesses, it is still cheaper for foreigners to buy them than to start from scratch. So the businesses wind up being very important for those who want to enter or expand in Brazil," he said.
Pactual estimates that companies must invest between $20 million and $60 million -- depending on the sector -- for every one percentage point of Brazilian market share.
"If you buy a business that already has market share, you can save yourself a lot of money," Fernandes said.
Purchases of local firms by international companies will help push foreign direct investment in Brazil to about $15.0 billion this year from $9.0 billion in 1996.
FOREIGNERS EYE PRIVATISATION, PACTUAL EYES FOREIGNERS
Pactual is also eyeing foreign interest in the sell-off of billions of dollars of federal, state and municipal assets, which until recently were mostly bought by local pension funds.
To date, foreign firms have accounted for just 13 percent of privatisations, a figure that could grow to 40 percent by the end of this year, Fernandes said.
He added that the participation of foreigners will grow even more in coming years, when Brazil's vast telecommunications and electrical sectors are taken to the auction block.
